title: ER Model & Relational Model
subtitle: Entities, attributes, relationships, cardinality, participation and relational-model vocabulary.
source: DBMS Crash Course Part 1 — Modules 1 to 4. Questions are independently crafted from the module concepts and exam-style patterns supplied for Bank SO IT.
instructions: Choose one answer for each question.
Questions are designed for IBPS SO IT, RRB Scale II IT, SBI SO and similar Computer Science/IT examinations.
Review the explanation, important point, exam trap and hint after submission.

questions.question: In an ER model, which component represents a distinguishable real-world object such as STUDENT or ACCOUNT?
questions.explanation: An entity represents a distinguishable real-world object or concept about which data is stored.
questions.importantPoint: Entity = object; attribute = property; relationship = association.
questions.examTrap: Do not confuse an entity with its descriptive properties.
questions.hint: Ask “what object are we storing information about?”

questions.question: In an ER model, DOB is stored for a STUDENT and AGE is calculated from DOB. What type of attribute is AGE?
questions.explanation: AGE can be computed from DOB, so it is a derived attribute.
questions.importantPoint: Derived attributes are obtained from other stored data.
questions.examTrap: A derived attribute need not be physically stored as an independent value.
questions.hint: Look for whether the value can be calculated from another attribute.

questions.question: Which ER notation represents a weak entity set in the standard Chen model?
questions.explanation: A weak entity is represented by a double rectangle in Chen ER notation.
questions.importantPoint: Weak entity → double rectangle.
questions.examTrap: A double diamond represents an identifying relationship, not the weak entity itself.
questions.hint: Focus on the entity-set symbol rather than the relationship symbol.

questions.question: Which ER notation represents an identifying relationship for a weak entity in the standard Chen model?
questions.explanation: The identifying relationship is represented by a double diamond in the standard Chen notation.
questions.importantPoint: Weak entity → double rectangle; identifying relationship → double diamond.
questions.examTrap: Do not swap the weak entity symbol with its identifying relationship.
questions.hint: Ask which symbol represents a relationship rather than an entity.

questions.question: In an ER model, a double line between an entity set and a relationship set indicates:
questions.explanation: A double line conventionally denotes total participation: every entity in the set must participate in the relationship.
questions.importantPoint: Total participation = mandatory participation.
questions.examTrap: Cardinality answers “how many”; participation answers “is participation required?”
questions.hint: Think “mandatory involvement.”

questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes cardinality from participation?

options.text: Cardinality specifies whether participation is mandatory; participation specifies the number of entities.
Cardinality specifies how many entities can participate; participation specifies whether participation is mandatory.
Both terms mean the same thing.
Cardinality applies only to attributes, while participation applies only to keys.

questions.explanation: Cardinality describes the number mapping such as 1:1 or 1:N, while participation describes whether every entity must participate.
questions.importantPoint: Cardinality = how many; participation = required or optional.
questions.examTrap: Do not use “total” and “partial” as cardinality terms.
questions.hint: Associate “how many?” with cardinality.

questions.question: A STUDENT can enroll in many COURSEs, and each COURSE can have many STUDENTs. What is the cardinality?
questions.explanation: Both sides can have many instances, so the relationship is many-to-many, written M:N.
questions.importantPoint: M:N means many on both sides.
questions.examTrap: 1:N would restrict one side to a single related entity.
questions.hint: Count the maximum possible related instances on both sides.

questions.question: A BANK_ACCOUNT must belong to exactly one CUSTOMER, while a CUSTOMER may have many BANK_ACCOUNTs. Which cardinality is most appropriate from CUSTOMER to BANK_ACCOUNT?
questions.explanation: One customer can have many accounts, while each account belongs to one customer, giving a 1:N relationship from CUSTOMER to BANK_ACCOUNT.
questions.importantPoint: 1:N means one instance on the first side can relate to many on the second.
questions.examTrap: Direction matters when describing 1:N versus N:1.
questions.hint: Read the relationship from CUSTOMER toward BANK_ACCOUNT.

questions.question: In the relational model, a tuple corresponds to a:
questions.explanation: A tuple is a row or record in a relation.
questions.importantPoint: Tuple = row; attribute = column.
questions.examTrap: Degree counts attributes, not tuples.
questions.hint: Use the table analogy: one horizontal record is a tuple.

questions.question: A relation has 7 attributes and 120 tuples. What are its degree and cardinality, respectively?
questions.explanation: Degree is the number of attributes (columns), 7; cardinality is the number of tuples (rows), 120.
questions.importantPoint: Degree → columns; cardinality → rows.
questions.examTrap: Do not reverse degree and cardinality.
questions.hint: Map attributes to columns and tuples to rows.

questions.question: Which statement about a domain is correct?

options.text: It is the number of rows in a relation.
It is the set of permitted values for an attribute.
It is the association between two entities.
It is the physical location of a table.

questions.explanation: A domain defines the allowable values or value set associated with an attribute.
questions.importantPoint: Domain = permitted values.
questions.examTrap: Cardinality and degree describe relation size/structure, not value restrictions.
questions.hint: Think “what values are allowed here?”

questions.question: A STUDENT entity has attributes Student_ID, Name, DOB and Phone_Numbers, where a student may have several phone numbers. Which attribute is naturally multivalued?
questions.explanation: If a single STUDENT may have several phone numbers, Phone_Numbers is multivalued.
questions.importantPoint: Multivalued attribute → multiple values for one entity instance.
questions.examTrap: A primary identifier such as Student_ID is normally single-valued.
questions.hint: Look for an attribute that can legitimately contain several values per entity.

questions.question: Which ER attribute notation is traditionally used for a derived attribute?
questions.explanation: A derived attribute is represented by a dashed ellipse in the standard Chen notation.
questions.importantPoint: Derived attribute → dashed ellipse.
questions.examTrap: Double ellipse is used for multivalued attributes in standard Chen notation.
questions.hint: Recall the distinction between stored and computed attributes.

questions.question: If an attribute uniquely identifies each entity instance in an ER model, it is commonly represented by:
questions.explanation: A key attribute is conventionally shown with its attribute name underlined in Chen notation.
questions.importantPoint: Key attribute → underlined attribute.
questions.examTrap: The rectangle represents an entity; the diamond represents a relationship.
questions.hint: Look for the notation used to mark a key.

questions.question: A relationship between DOCTOR and PATIENT records that a doctor treats a patient. Which ER component represents “treats”?
questions.explanation: “Treats” describes an association between two entity sets, so it is a relationship.
questions.importantPoint: Relationship = association between entity sets.
questions.examTrap: An attribute describes an entity; it does not represent the association itself.
questions.hint: Ask whether the term connects two entity types.

questions.question: A relation STUDENT(SID, Name, Dept) contains 50 rows currently. If one new student tuple is inserted, what happens to the relation’s cardinality, assuming the insertion succeeds?
questions.explanation: Cardinality counts rows/tuples, so adding one tuple changes it from 50 to 51.
questions.importantPoint: Insert row → cardinality changes; adding a column would change degree.
questions.examTrap: Degree is not affected by inserting a tuple.
questions.hint: Count rows before and after the insertion.

questions.question: Which statement is true for a 1:N relationship from DEPARTMENT to EMPLOYEE?

options.text: Every department must have exactly one employee.
An employee can belong to many departments under the stated relationship.
One department can be associated with many employees, while each employee is associated with at most one department.
Both sides must contain the same number of instances.

questions.explanation: In a 1:N relationship from DEPARTMENT to EMPLOYEE, one department can relate to many employees, while an employee is associated with at most one department through that relationship.
questions.importantPoint: The side marked 1 can map to many instances on the N side.
questions.examTrap: Cardinality does not automatically imply total participation.
questions.hint: Read the “1” and “N” from the stated direction.

questions.question: A COMPANY entity has a single registered address, but an employee may have multiple phone numbers. Which pair of attribute types is appropriate?
questions.explanation: A single address is simple/single-valued in the stated model, while multiple phone numbers make Phone multivalued.
questions.importantPoint: Attribute type depends on the number of values associated with one entity instance.
questions.examTrap: Do not infer multivalued status merely because a value can be stored as text.
questions.hint: Use the number of permitted values per entity instance.

questions.question: Which statement correctly relates a relation schema and a relation instance?

options.text: Schema is the current rows; instance is the column definition.
Schema describes structure; instance is the data present at a particular time.
Schema refers only to physical disk blocks.

questions.explanation: A relation schema defines attributes and structure, while a relation instance is the set of tuples present at a given time.
questions.importantPoint: Schema = structure; instance = current data.
questions.examTrap: An instance can change without changing the schema.
questions.hint: Separate “what the table looks like” from “what rows it currently contains.”

questions.question: A relationship is marked with total participation for EMPLOYEE in WORKS_FOR. What does this imply?

options.text: Every employee must participate in WORKS_FOR.
Every department must have exactly one employee.
Every employee must have multiple departments.

questions.explanation: Total participation means every entity in the specified EMPLOYEE set participates in the relationship.
questions.importantPoint: Total participation = mandatory participation for that entity set.
questions.examTrap: Participation does not by itself determine whether the relationship is 1:N or M:N.
questions.hint: Ask whether any employee may exist without participating.
